boundary_conditions.consequence_if_violated: If the share of transfer spending is low, proportional systems no longer lead to higher total primary spending; majoritarian systems do.
boundary_conditions.scope_text: The model also predicts higher total primary spending in proportional (majoritarian) systems when the share of transfer spending is high (low).

causal_claims.claim_text: Proportional electoral systems lead to higher transfer spending, while majoritarian systems lead to higher public good spending.
extraction_warnings: Theoretical prediction, not empirical estimate; no effect size provided.

supporting_spans.text: We present a theoretical model in which voters anticipating government policy-making under different electoral systems have an incentive to elect representatives more prone to transfer (public good) spending in proportional (majoritarian) systems.

causal_claims.claim_text: Total primary spending is higher in proportional systems when the share of transfer spending is high, and higher in majoritarian systems when the share of transfer spending is low.
extraction_warnings: Theoretical prediction, not empirical estimate; no effect size provided.

supporting_spans.text: The model also predicts higher total primary spending in proportional (majoritarian) systems when the share of transfer spending is high (low).

causal_claims.claim_text: Empirical investigation finds considerable support for the theoretical predictions linking electoral systems to public expenditure composition and size.
extraction_warnings: No specific effect sizes or statistical details provided; 'considerable support' is vague.

supporting_spans.text: After defining rigorous measures of proportionality to be used in the empirical investigation, we find considerable support for our predictions.

response.citation_summary: The paper studies the effects of electoral institutions on public expenditure in OECD and Latin American countries, presenting a theoretical model and empirical support.
extraction_warnings: Abstract-only source; no numeric effect sizes or detailed methodology available.
Causal claims are largely theoretical; empirical support is stated vaguely without specific estimates.

mechanisms.description: Voters anticipate policy-making under different electoral systems and elect representatives who favor transfer spending in proportional systems and public good spending in majoritarian systems, shaping expenditure composition and total spending.

response.methodology: Theoretical model with empirical investigation using rigorous measures of proportionality; no specific econometric method described in the abstract.
